meta.topic: FX provider role in instant cross-border payments

problem:
Meridian Bank offers instant cross-border payments but does not hold liquidity in every settlement currency its customers need. It relies on an FX provider to source quotes, lock rates, execute conversion and supply settlement currency. The arrangement works on quiet days, but on a busy morning the cracks show: a quote expires while screening runs, the provider cannot supply the settlement currency at the required time, and a payment executes at a rate the customer never accepted.

The bank and the provider each assume the other owns the risk. The bank assumes the provider guarantees the rate and the liquidity; the provider assumes the bank will only send executable instructions inside the quote window. Neither assumption is written down, so the customer bears the consequence when the two assumptions collide.

The bank must define the FX provider role precisely: quote sourcing, rate locking, execution, liquidity and exception handling, with clear ownership of the risk at each step.
solution:
Write the FX provider role as a contract with five parts: quote sourcing, rate locking, execution, liquidity and exception handling. Quote sourcing states which currencies, which hours, which quote validity windows and which tolerances apply. Rate locking states what is locked, for how long, and what happens at expiry. Execution states the exact instruction format, the single consumption rule for a quote, and the revalidation the bank performs before sending. Liquidity states the settlement currency the provider will supply, the cut offs, and what happens when it cannot supply it. Exception handling states who notifies whom, within what time, and who bears the cost of a failed or late execution.

Bind every quote to the payment as an immutable snapshot with quote ID, currency pair, amounts, rate, spread, fees, expiry and execution conditions, and store the customer consent evidence beside it. Revalidate at execution and stop for a fresh quote and fresh consent when the quote has expired or the rate has moved beyond tolerance. Enforce single consumption so one quote cannot fund two payments, and reject any provider execution that does not match the locked quote.

Distinguish FX conversion from settlement currency availability. A good rate does not help if the settlement currency is not available at the required time. The bank must check liquidity before promising an instant outcome, hold or queue the payment under a documented rule when liquidity is short, and never promise a settlement time the liquidity position cannot support.

Design the legs separately. The customer leg, the FX conversion and the settlement leg each have their own state, and a failure in one leg must not silently change another. If the sender is debited and the destination leg then fails, the bank establishes whether the debit is provisional or final, returns or compensates funds under the defined process, and ensures exactly one financial effect.

decision.question: Meridian Bank sends an FX instruction to its provider after the quoted rate has expired, and the provider executes at the current market rate. The customer complains that the beneficiary received less than the disclosed amount. Who should have prevented this, and how?

options.label: A
options.detail: The bank, by binding the quote ID, rate, amounts and expiry to the payment, revalidating at execution, and never sending an expired quote for execution without fresh customer consent.

options.label: B
options.detail: Nobody, because market rates always move.

options.label: C
options.detail: The provider, by refusing to execute any instruction outside its quote window.

options.label: D
options.detail: The customer, by accepting that any rate may apply.

decisionRationale: Option A is correct because the bank owns the payment instruction and must revalidate the quote at execution and obtain fresh consent when terms change. Option C is wrong as a sole answer because the bank must not send an expired instruction in the first place, even though the provider should also reject it. Option B is wrong because rate movement is expected and must be governed by a quote contract, not accepted as an excuse. Option D is wrong because the customer accepted a specific disclosed rate, not any rate.

steps.title: Requests a cross-border payment with source and destination currencies
Sources a quote with rate, fees, amounts and a defined validity window
Accepts the quote with the full disclosure of rate, fees and final amounts
Binds the quote snapshot and consent to the payment and checks settlement currency liquidity
Runs sanctions, AML and fraud screening within the quote window
Revalidates the quote at execution and sends the execution instruction to the FX provider
Executes the conversion and supplies the settlement currency
Sends the payment onward and confirms the final rate, amounts and value date to the customer

happy: The customer accepts a quote with rate, fees and final amounts disclosed. Liquidity is confirmed, screening completes inside the validity window, the quote revalidates at execution, the provider executes at the locked rate, the settlement currency is supplied, the payment reaches the beneficiary, and the confirmation shows the quote ID, rate and value date.

negative.title: Quote expires before execution
negative.detail: Screening or routing delays execution beyond the quote validity window. Pause execution, obtain a fresh quote, and proceed only on fresh customer consent or cancel cleanly with no debit.

negative.title: Liquidity shortfall
negative.detail: The provider cannot supply the settlement currency at the required time. Hold or queue the payment under the documented rule, tell the customer the realistic timing, and do not promise an instant outcome the liquidity cannot support.

negative.title: Duplicate quote consumption
negative.detail: The same quote ID is presented for a second payment. Reject the second use, log the attempt, and require a fresh quote for the second payment.

negative.title: Destination failure after sender debit
negative.detail: The destination leg fails after the sender is debited and conversion has executed. Establish whether the debit is provisional or final, return or compensate funds under the defined process, and ensure exactly one financial effect.

technical: Store the quote snapshot immutably with quote ID, provider ID, currency pair, rate, amounts, spread, fees, expiry timestamp, tolerance, liquidity confirmation and consent timestamp, linked to the payment by correlation ID. Enforce single consumption with a unique constraint on the quote ID, and validate every provider execution response against the locked quote before posting. Record liquidity checks, revalidations and provider responses as structured events, and keep the customer leg, the conversion and the settlement leg as separate records with their own state machines. Use idempotency keys on every provider call so a retry cannot execute twice.

messages.title: Customer credit transfer for the converted payment
Financial institution transfer for the settlement leg where the model requires it
Status report for the payment and settlement legs
Internal contract binding the quote to the payment, not a scheme message

accounting: Debit the customer account for the total agreed debit, credit the FX conversion account at the locked rate, and credit the settlement account for the destination amount, with fees as separate entries. If the quote expires and the customer declines a fresh quote, reverse any reservation exactly once with no conversion posting. A liquidity shortfall moves the payment to a held worklist with an ageing service level, and a provider execution that does not match the locked quote is stopped for investigation before any customer posting. Treasury monitors provider quote expiry rates, liquidity coverage by currency and corridor, and execution mismatches as provider performance measures.

scenarios.then: the payment is not silently executed at a different rate. the customer is asked to accept a fresh quote

scenarios.given: a quote ID has already been consumed
scenarios.when: the same quote ID is presented again
scenarios.then: the second use is rejected. a fresh quote is required

questions.question: What must be bound to the payment as one FX quote contract?
options: Quote ID, currency pair, amounts, rate, fees, expiry and execution conditions
questions.explanation: The quote contract includes the ID, pair, amounts, rate, fees, spread, expiry and execution conditions.

questions.question: What is the difference between FX conversion and settlement currency availability?
options: A good rate does not help if the settlement currency is not available at the required time
questions.explanation: Conversion sets the rate; liquidity determines whether the settlement currency can actually be supplied when needed.

questions.question: What should happen if a quote ID is presented for a second payment?
options: Reject the second use and require a fresh quote
Accept it, since the rate is already known
Execute both payments at the same rate
questions.explanation: A quote must be consumed once; a second use must be rejected.

questions.question: Who bears FX risk between quote acceptance and settlement?
options: The party defined by the quote contract, with the bank revalidating at execution and seeking fresh consent when terms change
questions.explanation: Risk ownership is defined by the quote contract, and the bank must revalidate and obtain fresh consent when the locked terms no longer hold.
